1171.event_title: Mozart weeps after Aloysia Weber turns away from him
1171.event: On his way to Paris in 1777 the young Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart met the Weber family in Mannheim and fell in love with the gifted singer Aloysia Weber, who was his pupil. When he reached Munich on his way home in late 1778, she had turned away from him, though she had once returned some of his affection. In a letter to his father dated 29 December 1778, Mozart wrote that today he could only weep and that his heart was too full of tears; four years later he married her sister Constanze.
1171.explanation: Mozart's own letter records how a love that began with delight in seeing and hearing Aloysia ended, for the moment, in tears.
1171.tie_back: The kural asks why the eyes that first showed the heroine her beloved now weep for him, and Mozart's tears in Munich came from the same love his eyes had first welcomed in Mannheim.
1171._accuracy_note: A documented case of love begun by seeing and ending in weeping, though it is a young man's rejection rather than a wife's separation from her husband.

1172.event_title: Robert Burns writes Ae Fond Kiss on parting from Agnes McLehose
1172.event: Robert Burns and Agnes McLehose of Glasgow carried on a passionate but platonic correspondence under the pen names Sylvander and Clarinda, since she was married. In December 1791, as she prepared to sail to Jamaica to try to reconcile with her husband, the two met for the last time, and Burns wrote the song Ae Fond Kiss for her on their parting. Decades later Agnes wrote in her journal that she had parted with Burns in 1791, never to meet again in this world.
1172.explanation: The song's famous lament is that the lovers would never have been broken-hearted if they had never met, a reflection on how a love so gladly begun can lead to grief.
1172.tie_back: The kural blames the eyes that once gazed at the beloved without weighing what would follow and now suffer for it, which is the same thought Burns put into his farewell song.
1172._accuracy_note: The song's regret over a meeting that led to heartbreak closely matches the kural's reasoning, though the relationship was between a poet and a married correspondent rather than husband and wife.

1173.event_title: Berlioz's obsession with the actress Harriet Smithson
1173.event: In 1827 the composer Hector Berlioz saw the Irish actress Harriet Smithson play Ophelia in an English-language Hamlet in Paris and became fixated on her. He waited at the stage door, bombarded her with love letters that she ignored, and rented rooms near her theatre, though neither spoke the other's language. He poured the unrequited passion into his Symphonie fantastique, premiered in December 1830; the two married in October 1833, but the marriage was unhappy and they later agreed to live apart.
1173.explanation: Berlioz's headlong pursuit, set off by a single look at an actress on stage, became one of music history's most famous examples of love at first sight turning into torment.
1173.tie_back: The kural laughs at eyes that rushed of their own accord to look and now of their own accord weep, and Berlioz's eager gaze at the stage and the years of anguish that followed fit that rueful humour.
1173._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of love sparked by the eyes and the self-made suffering that followed, though Berlioz was a pursuing admirer, not a wife parted from her husband.

1174.event_title: Theodore Roosevelt's diary on the day his wife died
1174.event: On 14 February 1884 Theodore Roosevelt's mother died of typhoid fever early in the morning, and his wife, Alice Hathaway Lee Roosevelt, died that afternoon in the same house, two days after giving birth to their daughter. In his pocket diary Roosevelt marked a large X on the page and wrote, The light has gone out of my life. He chose never to speak Alice's name again and did not mention her in his autobiography.
1174.explanation: Roosevelt's single line and his lifelong silence show a grief so deep that it could not be cured and was never again put into words.
1174.tie_back: The kural speaks of eyes that have wept until no tears remain, leaving behind a sickness with no remedy, and Roosevelt's eight-word entry and later silence suggest that kind of exhausted, incurable sorrow.
1174._accuracy_note: The incurable grief fits, but the loss was by death and the kural's specific idea that the eyes caused the sickness is missing, so this is next-best.

1175.event_title: Juliette Drouet's fifty years of daily letters to Victor Hugo
1175.place: Paris, France, and the Channel Islands
1175.event: From 1833 until her death in 1883, the actress Juliette Drouet wrote to the writer Victor Hugo every day, producing about 22,000 letters over fifty years. Around 17,000 of them are now held by the Bibliotheque nationale de France and others by institutions such as the University of Leeds. Scholars describe her as Hugo's soulmate, collaborator, first reader and copyist, and her letters as a kind of journal of their relationship.
1175.explanation: Her letters are a record of a love so large that it filled a page or more every day for half a century.
1175.tie_back: The kural speaks of a love-sickness too great even for the sea to hold, and Drouet's ocean of letters, written day after day for fifty years, gives that size a measurable form.
1175._accuracy_note: The sheer scale of devotion matches the kural's love greater than the sea, but its focus on sleepless, suffering eyes is not documented in these sources.

1176.event_title: Cleopatra meets Mark Antony at Tarsus
1176.event: In 41 BCE the Roman general Mark Antony summoned Cleopatra, queen of Egypt, to Tarsus to answer charges that she had helped his enemies. According to Plutarch, she sailed up the river Cydnus in a gilded barge with purple sails, and Antony was so taken with her that he returned with her to Alexandria. Their alliance ended in defeat at the Battle of Actium in 31 BCE, and both died in Egypt the following year.
1176.explanation: Cleopatra came to Tarsus to win over Antony, and the attachment she created drew her, as well as him, into the same disaster.
1176.tie_back: The kural takes grim satisfaction that the eyes which caused the heroine's love-sickness have fallen into the same suffering, much as Cleopatra, who captivated Antony, was caught in the ruin that their love brought on them both.
1176._accuracy_note: The idea of the one who caused love's suffering being trapped in it too is only loosely present, and the details of the barge come from Plutarch's later account, so this is a next-best fit.

1177.event_title: Rembrandt draws Saskia days after their betrothal
1177.place: Dutch Republic (now the Netherlands); drawing now in Berlin, Germany
1177.event: On 6 June 1633 Rembrandt became engaged to Saskia van Uylenburgh, the cousin of his business partner Hendrick Uylenburgh. On 8 June he made a silverpoint drawing of her, inscribed in Dutch that it was drawn of his wife when she was 21 years old, on the third day after their betrothal; it is now in the Kupferstichkabinett in Berlin. After three children who did not survive infancy, Saskia gave birth to their son Titus, and Rembrandt's later decline in productivity followed her death.
1177.explanation: The tender drawing preserves the moment when Rembrandt gazed on his bride-to-be with delight, before the losses that later came to the marriage.
1177.tie_back: The kural speaks of eyes that once gazed on the beloved with melting, eager longing and must now ache, and Rembrandt's betrothal drawing is a record of such a loving gaze that later turned to grief.
1177._accuracy_note: The drawing documents the loving gaze, but the later aching of the eyes is only implied by Saskia's early death, so the fit is next-best.

1178.event_title: Izumi Shikibu asks for one last meeting
1178.event: Izumi Shikibu, one of the leading women poets of the Heian court, wrote a poem addressed to her beloved when she believed her life was drawing to a close. In it she asks for just one more meeting with him, so that she may carry its memory with her beyond this world. The poem was later chosen as number 56 of the Hyakunin Isshu anthology.
1178.explanation: Her poem became one of Japan's best-known expressions of the simple, overwhelming need to see the beloved once more.
1178.tie_back: The kural says the heroine's eyes cannot rest without seeing him, and Izumi Shikibu's plea for a single last meeting shows that same longing to see the beloved again.
1178._accuracy_note: The longing to see the beloved matches the kural well, but the kural's reproach that he loved without truly caring is not reflected in the poem.

1179.event_title: Franz Kafka's engagements to Felice Bauer
1179.place: Prague (now Czech Republic) and Berlin, Germany
1179.event: Franz Kafka met Felice Bauer at the home of his friend Max Brod in Prague on 13 August 1912. Over the next five years he sent her more than five hundred letters and postcards, and the two became engaged twice, but each engagement was broken off, the second and last time in December 1917. Felice later married another man and, years afterwards, gave Kafka's letters to Schocken publishers, who published them in the 1960s.
1179.explanation: Kafka's letters show a man who longed for Felice when they were apart and drew back when marriage came close, so that neither distance nor nearness gave him peace.
1179.tie_back: The kural says the eyes cannot sleep when the beloved is away, nor when he comes, and suffer in between, which describes the restless back-and-forth of Kafka's two engagements.
1179._accuracy_note: The pattern of unrest both apart and together fits the kural, but the sources document the broken engagements and letters, not literal sleeplessness, and it is the man's unrest rather than the woman's.

1180.event_title: Princess Margaret's gesture at the coronation reveals her romance
1180.event: At the coronation of her sister, Queen Elizabeth II, on 2 June 1953, Princess Margaret was seen brushing a piece of lint from the uniform jacket of Group Captain Peter Townsend, her late father's former equerry. A journalist noticed the moment, and it set off public speculation about their relationship. Because Townsend was divorced, the match was opposed, and in 1955 Margaret issued a statement that she would not marry him.
1180.explanation: One small, unguarded gesture in front of the world's cameras revealed a private love that the palace had kept quiet.
1180.tie_back: The kural says the secret in a lover's heart is no secret to the town when her own eyes beat it out like a drum, and Margaret's single gesture at the coronation announced her hidden love to everyone watching.
1180._accuracy_note: A close illustration of private love betrayed in public by an unguarded sign, though it was a gesture rather than the eyes themselves.
